title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Introduction
content: Alveoli represent the terminal units of the respiratory tree, expanding during inhalation to facilitate oxygen uptake and contracting during exhalation to expel carbon dioxide. At this microscopic air–liquid interface, a balance exists between inward collapsing forces, primarily generated by surface tension, and outward recoil forces provided by the lung parenchyma. Surface tension at the alveolar lining constitutes a major determinant of lung recoil and critically influences alveolar stability and gas-exchange efficiency.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Introduction
content: Recent computational and experimental evidence confirms that elevated alveolar surface tension, whether secondary to surfactant deficiency or structural injury, produces altered airflow dynamics, increased shear stress on alveolar walls, and heterogeneity in alveolar expansion. [1] Emerging work in lung injury models also demonstrates that disrupted surfactant homeostasis correlates with increased alveolar surface tension, structural collapse, and worsened gas-exchange outcomes. Given these mechanistic insights, a thorough understanding of alveolar tension remains fundamental for interpreting normal pulmonary physiology and the pathophysiology of disorders such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), ventilator-induced lung injury, and surfactant dysfunction.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Issues of Concern
content: Elevated alveolar surface tension remains a significant pathophysiologic concern in acute and chronic lung injury, as it can initiate alveolar collapse, impair gas exchange, and promote ventilator-induced lung injury. Models of ARDS demonstrate that surfactant inactivation and plasma-rich edema fluid increase surface tension, contributing to heterogeneous alveolar inflation, increased shear stress, and subsequent epithelial injury. [2]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Issues of Concern
content: Recent studies in epithelial biology show that impaired surfactant processing in type II alveolar epithelial cells directly elevates alveolar surface tension and promotes collapse. Notch1-driven loss of napsin A disrupts the processing of surfactant proteins B and C, resulting in dysfunctional films, increased surface tension, and endoplasmic reticulum–stress–mediated epithelial injury. [3] Direct in situ ARDS experiments indicate that cell debris, mucins, acid, and secretory phospholipase A2 (sPLA2) markedly elevate alveolar surface tension, impair surfactant performance, and predispose alveoli to collapse and ventilation-induced injury. [4]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Issues of Concern
content: Measurement of airway surface-liquid rheology and surface tension reveals substantial intersubject variability and technical limitations in vivo , posing a barrier to translating micromechanical insights into bedside strategies for lung-protective ventilation. [5] In genetic deficiency of surfactant protein B (SP-B), experimental data demonstrate that high surface tension precedes fluid accumulation and alveolar epithelial injury, suggesting a “tipping-point” dynamic in which alveolar recruitability fails and leakage accelerates. [6] These findings indicate that subtle increases in alveolar tension may not manifest in static compliance changes until late in disease progression, emphasizing the importance of early intervention, precise ventilator settings, and consideration of surfactant dysfunction in patients with at-risk lungs.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Structure
content: Alveoli are classically described as a cluster of grapes, with each alveolus considered a separate entity from the surrounding structures. However, recent histologic research reveals a more complex architecture. Numerous connections between alveoli create an intricate system of airflow within the distal airways. High-resolution synchrotron imaging demonstrates that alveoli form a highly interconnected network rather than isolated balloon-like sacs. Alveolar shapes are polygonal with flat sides, and each alveolus shares a common wall with neighboring units. The overall appearance more closely resembles foam or froth than balloons. [7]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Structure
content: The wall separating 2 adjacent alveoli, the interalveolar septum, consists of a single layer of alveolar epithelial cells, capillary endothelial cells, and interstitial tissues. Two distinct alveolar epithelial cell types exist: type I and type II pneumocytes. Type I pneumocytes cover approximately 95% of the alveolar surface and provide an optimized environment for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant, a substance that reduces surface tension, as discussed later in this activity. Type II pneumocytes also function as progenitor cells capable of differentiating into both alveolar cell types following lung injury. [8]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: The balance between expanding and collapsing forces determines alveolar size at any given moment. Lung recoil describes the tendency of alveoli to return to their resting state after inflation. The primary determinant of lung recoil is surface tension, a force generated by water molecules at the liquid surface. Surface tension arises at any air–liquid interface, such as the alveolar lining, and acts to minimize surface area.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: The composition of lung tissue represents the other principal determinant of recoil. High collagen and elastin fiber content confers substantial elastic properties. Although these collapsing forces are essential for exhalation, they must be counteracted by expanding forces at end-expiration to prevent alveolar collapse. A major force maintaining alveolar patency is the extensive collagen extracellular matrix within the interalveolar septa. The extracellular matrix contains fibroblasts that generate radial traction, exerting forces away from the center of each alveolus to maintain inflation.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: Surfactant, produced by type II pneumocytes, comprises another critical factor preventing alveolar collapse. A full understanding of pulmonary surfactant function and its effect on surface tension requires knowledge of the physical interactions between water molecules.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: Water is a polar molecule, with the oxygen atom carrying a greater negative charge than the 2 covalently bonded hydrogen atoms. The electronegativity of oxygen produces a partial negative charge on one side of the molecule and a partial positive charge on the opposite side. In the presence of neighboring water molecules, negatively charged regions attract positively charged regions of adjacent molecules. These interactions generate surface tension, a cohesive force that pulls water molecules together. Within the alveoli, the water lining the interior surface experiences inward-directed surface tension. In the absence of a counteracting mechanism, this force would lead to alveolar collapse.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: Humans, along with many other mammals, possess a mechanism that lowers surface tension in alveoli and distal airways. Type II pneumocytes secrete pulmonary surfactant, which reduces surface tension. Surfactant consists of approximately 90% lipids and 10% proteins. Surfactant proteins serve diverse functions, many of which remain under investigation and are beyond the scope of this activity. [9]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: Surfactant lipids play a central role in reducing surface tension and are primarily phospholipids. These biomolecules contain a polar "head" and two nonpolar "tails" (see Image. Basic Structure of a Phospholipid). Water, a polar compound, interacts readily with other polar substances, which are termed "hydrophilic." Nonpolar molecules do not mix with water and are termed "hydrophobic." Phospholipids, possessing both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, are classified as amphipathic.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: When amphipathic molecules interact with water, the hydrophilic head forms transient bonds with charged regions of adjacent water molecules, whereas the hydrophobic tails repel water and orient toward each other. This arrangement forms surfactant "spheres," with heads facing outward toward water and tails inward. Collections of these surfactant structures interrupt interactions between water molecules, thereby lowering surface tension. Recent biophysical studies demonstrate that pulmonary surfactant rapidly adsorbs to the alveolar air–liquid interface, forming a stable film that minimizes surface tension during tidal ventilation. [10]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: The phospholipid most abundant in surfactant is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC). While other lipids and proteins contribute to surface tension regulation, DPPC constitutes the primary lipid produced by type II pneumocytes. [11] In the absence of DPPC, collapsing forces within alveoli and distal airways would exceed expanding forces, leading to complete alveolar collapse and impaired gas exchange.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: Laplace's law provides another relevant concept regarding surface tension. Historically, the pressure required to counteract alveolar collapse was considered directly proportional to twice the surface tension and inversely proportional to alveolar radius (P = 2T/r). This equation, known as Laplace’s Law, applies only to spherical structures. More recent research demonstrates that alveoli are polygonal, highly interconnected units rather than isolated spheres. Given this geometry, Laplace’s Law cannot be directly applied to calculate the collapsing force of surface tension in alveoli.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Function
content: Nonetheless, the principle that pressure in a sphere is directly proportional to twice the surface tension and inversely proportional to the radius (P = 2T/r) is important to consider. Two spheres of different sizes illustrate the concept. Pressure increases as the radius decreases, according to Laplace's Law. If the 2 spheres are connected by a tube, the smaller sphere would empty into the larger one due to the pressure gradient. Applied to alveoli, this principle suggests that smaller alveoli should empty into larger ones, potentially causing lung collapse.

As the alveolar radius decreases, surfactant molecules become more concentrated in smaller alveoli, increasing their effectiveness in reducing surface tension. title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Pathophysiology
content: Surfactant is essential for preventing alveolar and distal airway collapse. Processes that disrupt surfactant production, function, or metabolism can severely compromise pulmonary function. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, primarily observed in premature neonates, was the first disease linked to surfactant deficiency. Lung immaturity in these infants results in insufficient surfactant production. Consequently, alveoli and distal airways fail to remain open during expiration, impairing effective oxygen–carbon dioxide exchange. Historically, management relied on administering 100% oxygen until endogenous surfactant production reached sufficient levels.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Pathophysiology
content: Additional conditions associated with surfactant abnormalities include ARDS, alveolar proteinosis, obstructive lung diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung diseases including pulmonary fibrosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, infectious processes such as pneumonia and AIDS, and complications in patients who smoke.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Pathophysiology
content: ARDS represents another context in which surface tension plays a critical role. Widespread pulmonary inflammation leads to rapid respiratory failure, commonly triggered by acute pancreatitis, pneumonia, trauma, or sepsis. Alveolar and capillary damage permits leakage of fluids and proteins into the alveoli. These proteins disrupt surfactant composition and function, diminishing the ability of this protective substance to counteract surface tension. The resulting alveolar collapse produces abnormalities in gas exchange. [13]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Clinical Significance
content: Multiple interventions now exist to manage neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. These strategies aim either to reduce disease severity or to prevent its occurrence. For prevention, pregnant women at risk of preterm delivery should receive antenatal glucocorticoids to enhance fetal lung maturity and stimulate surfactant production. [14]

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Clinical Significance
content: Respiratory support with positive end-expiratory pressure maintains airway patency at end-expiration and prevents alveolar collapse in affected neonates. [15] Exogenous surfactant replacement therapy provides temporary supplementation until endogenous surfactant production reaches adequate levels.

title: Physiology, Alveolar Tension -- Clinical Significance
content: A variety of other pulmonary diseases may involve abnormalities in surfactant production, function, or metabolism. At present, exogenous surfactant therapy is not routinely applied in these conditions. Recent studies indicate that impaired alveolar type II stem cell regeneration exposes alveoli to sustained mechanical tension, activating an injury–fibrosis loop driven by transforming growth factor β and promoting progressive peripheral-to-central pulmonary fibrosis. [16]
